sentences.text: The skull of Rukwasuchus features ellipsoidal openings, which differ from the nearly circular holes seen in the related genus Stolokrosuchus.
Unlike modern crocodiles, the optic recess in this animal does not close at the back but instead opens downward.
A pronounced U-shape is formed by the supraoccipital bone, which bends downward due to pressure from the overlying parietal bone.
The otoccipitals dominate the back of the skull, creating a wide U-shaped joint with the supraoccipital between the temporal openings.
The laterosphenoid bone builds the front side wall of the braincase and is made of two layers separated by a ridge.
The front part of the parabasisphenoid is a subrectangular plate that widens toward the top and connects to other braincase structures.
Specific ridges on the jaw joint are shared traits with other peirosaurians like Hamadasuchus and Montealtosuchus.
The type specimen, cataloged as RRBP 08630, was gathered in 2008 at the Namba 2 site.
All known fossils were discovered roughly 25 kilometers south of Lake Rukwa in southwestern Tanzania.
The species was officially named by Joseph J. W. Sertich and Patrick M. O'Connor in 2014.
Although the main specimen lacks teeth, several teeth from the same geological layer have been tentatively linked to this taxon.
Computed tomography scans have revealed large portions of the internal brain mold, though some details remain hidden by damage or rock matrix.
Researchers describe Rukwasuchus as a medium-to-large-bodied creature.
Certain brain features suggest this animal may have spent more time on land than some of its semi-aquatic relatives.
Phylogenetic studies generally place Rukwasuchus within the clade Peirosauria.
Its family placement is debated, with some placing it in Peirosauridae and others viewing it as a basal member of Itasuchidae.
It is a monotypic genus, meaning it contains only the single species Rukwasuchus yajabalijekundu.
Analyses suggest this lineage split after Kinesuchus and Stolokrosuchus but before most South American forms.
More recent work by Ruiz et al. (2024) and Wilberg et al. (2025) places it in either the subfamily Pepesuchinae or the family Itasuchidae.
Fossils are found exclusively in the Namba Member of the Galula Formation in Tanzania.
The animal lived between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago during the Cenomanian to Campanian stages.
The environment was wetter and sub-humid, featuring paleosols consistent with an open forest that followed a shift from the drier underlying Mtuka Member.
